title: Impact of Rent Control Expansion on Urban Rental Prices

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

We will use a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach to estimate the causal impact of rent control expansion on rental prices. The DID method is suitable here because we have a treatment group (districts with rent control expansion) and a control group (districts without rent control expansion), and we can observe the rental prices before and after the policy change.

The key assumption in DID is that, in the absence of the treatment, the treatment and control groups would have followed the same trend. This assumption is often referred to as the "parallel trends" assumption.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(plm)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s38_data.csv")

# Convert the data to a panel data frame
pdata <- pdata.frame(data, index = c("unit_id", "period"))

# Run the DID regression
did_model <- plm(y ~ treat_x_post, data = pdata, model = "within")

# Print the coefficient for the treatment effect
summary(did_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Estimate"]

# Robustness check: Clustered standard errors
coeftest(did_model, vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1"))
```

## 3. Expected Findings

We expect the coefficient on the `treat_x_post` variable to be negative, as rent control policies are designed to limit rental price increases. The magnitude of the effect will depend on the strength of the rent control policies and the responsiveness of rental prices to these policies. Given the limited number of observations, the estimated effect may be imprecise, but we expect it to provide some indication of the impact of rent control expansion on rental prices.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log rental prices over time between treated and untreated districts.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The expansion of rent control policies led to a decrease in log rental prices in treated districts.
